title: Weather, Land and Water
overview: Weather is the subject English speakers use to open conversations with strangers, which makes it more useful than its content suggests. This unit gives you the one form English uses both to predict and to decide in the moment, the vocabulary for describing where a place is and what it is like, and the two words that join a reason to a result. It ends with a forecast and a weather warning, because the difference between those two documents is the difference between information and instruction.
learningPath: Read and listen to the Lesson. There are three patterns.
Open Patterns. Card 1 does two jobs — the second one is the surprise.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is a forecast and a warning.
Do the Practice. Practice 2 is where because and so get swapped.
Record yourself predicting the weather and describing a place.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.
lectureScript:
Three patterns, and the first one is a tense you have been hearing since Unit 1 without being taught it.
Will. And like the present continuous in Unit 10, it does two jobs that most courses separate.
The form first, because it is the easiest in English. Will plus the plain verb. Nothing changes for he, she or it.
I will go. She will go. They will go. No -s, ever.
The contraction is 'll, and you will hear it far more often than the full word. I'll, she'll, we'll. And the negative is will not, contracted to won't — which does not sound like will at all, and is worth saying aloud a few times.
Job one: prediction. What you think is going to happen.
It will rain tomorrow. It will be cold at the weekend. The journey will take about two hours.
This is what forecasts are made of, and it is the use most courses teach.
Job two, and this is the one that gets missed. A decision you make at the moment of speaking.
Somebody says the shop closes in ten minutes. You say: I'll go now.
Somebody says we need more chairs. You say: I'll get them.
You did not plan that. You decided it as you spoke, and English marks that with will.
That is a genuinely useful distinction, because it tells you which form to use when. If you already arranged it, that is the present continuous from Unit 10 — I'm leaving on Tuesday. If you are deciding right now, it is will — I'll leave now.
So the pair is: arranged before, present continuous. Decided this second, will.
Unit 15 will put will, going to and the present continuous side by side, and choosing between them is the whole point of that unit. Here you only need will, doing its two jobs.
One small thing about probability. English rarely predicts flatly. It hedges, and the two words it uses most are probably and definitely.
It will probably rain. It definitely won't snow.
Notice where probably goes: after will, before the verb. It will probably rain. Not it probably will rain — though you will hear that too, and neither will cause a problem.
Second pattern: describing a place. This is vocabulary and one structure, and the structure is worth having.
A place description answers three things in order: where it is, what is around it, what it is like.
Where: It's in the north of the country. It's on the coast. It's about fifty kilometres from the city.
What is around: There are mountains behind it. There's a river through the middle.
What it is like: It's quite dry in summer. It's a small place and it's very quiet.
The useful structure there is there is and there are, which you use for saying what exists in a place. There is a river. There are mountains. Singular takes is, plural takes are, and it is one of the most useful structures in English for description of any kind.
Third pattern: because and so. These join a reason to a result, and they are opposite ways round.
Because introduces the reason. So introduces the result.
We stayed at home because it was raining. Reason comes after because.
It was raining, so we stayed at home. Result comes after so.
Same two facts, same meaning, opposite order. The rain is the reason; staying at home is the result.
That is the whole rule, and the test is simple: what comes after because is why. What comes after so is what happened.
One punctuation note. When so joins two full sentences, English usually puts a comma before it. It was raining, so we stayed at home. Because does not normally take a comma when it comes in the middle.
And one warning: do not use both in the same sentence. Because it was raining, so we stayed at home is a very common error and it is wrong in English — you use one or the other, never both.
Go to Patterns.

The weather has been good all week.

There was no rain for three weeks.

readings.title: Why the Weather Is Worth Learning
readings.passage:
The weather is not an interesting subject, and English speakers talk about it constantly. That is worth understanding rather than finding strange.
It is the safe opening. When two people who do not know each other need to say something, the weather is the subject nobody can be offended by, nobody has to know anything about, and everybody can contribute to. It is not really a conversation about the weather. It is a way of establishing that a conversation is possible.
So when somebody in a queue says cold today, isn't it, they are not telling you the temperature. They are opening a door, and the expected reply is agreement plus one small addition. Yes, and it was so warm last week. That is the whole exchange, and it is complete.
What does not work is a full and accurate answer. If somebody says cold today and you reply with the actual temperature, the exchange stops, because you have treated an opening as a question.
This is worth knowing for a practical reason. Learners often avoid these exchanges because they feel like small talk with no content and they are hard to prepare for. But they are the most predictable exchanges in English. The subject is fixed, the structure is fixed, and agreement is almost always the right move. Of all the conversations you will have, this is the one you can rehearse most reliably.
One small warning. Agreement is expected but exaggeration is not. If somebody says it is a bit cold and you say it is the coldest day of my life, that is a joke, and it may or may not land. Matching their level is safer.

readings.title: A Forecast Is Not a Warning
readings.passage:
Two kinds of weather document exist and they ask different things of you.
A forecast tells you what will probably happen. It uses will, it hedges with probably and mainly and in places, and it expects you to make your own decisions. Rain in the north, becoming dry later. That is information. Whether you take a coat is up to you.
A warning tells you to do something. It is issued when weather is likely to cause harm, and it usually contains instructions rather than predictions. Do not travel unless necessary. Avoid the coast road. That is not information — it is an instruction, and the wording changes to match.
The language tells you which one you are reading, and there are three signals.
Modal verbs. A forecast says will and may. A warning says do not and avoid.
Hedging. A forecast hedges constantly — probably, mainly, in places, at times. A warning does not hedge, because the point of it is to be unambiguous.
Colour and heading. Warnings are usually labelled, and the label carries a level. Learn the levels used where you live, because they mean specific things and the difference between them is the difference between inconvenience and danger.
One practical note. A forecast can be wrong without anybody having failed, because it is a probability. A warning being wrong is different — warnings are issued when the risk is high enough to act on even if it does not happen. So the fact that the last warning came to nothing is not a reason to ignore the next one, and that is the single most common mistake people make with them.

readings.title: The Forecast, and the Warning
readings.setting: A regional forecast, and a warning issued the same evening.
readings.passage:
FORECAST - Thursday
  Northfield and surrounding area

  MORNING
    Fog in the valley, clearing by 09:00.
    Cold. 4 degrees.

  AFTERNOON
    Cloud increasing from the west.
    Rain arriving after 15:00, heavy in
    places. 9 degrees.

  EVENING
    Rain continuing. Wind strengthening
    from the west, strongest on the coast.
    7 degrees.

  FRIDAY
    Rain clearing early. Bright and cold.
    Snow on the hills above 400m.

-----------------------------------------

  ** WEATHER WARNING - AMBER **
  Issued 18:40 Thursday
  Valid 20:00 Thursday to 06:00 Friday

  STRONG WIND

  Do not travel on the coast road
  between Northfield and the harbour.

  Avoid parking under trees.

  Some power cuts are likely.

  Ferry services are cancelled until
  further notice.

  AMBER means: be prepared. There is a
  risk to travel and to property.
  RED means: take action. There is a
  risk to life.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say weather talk is not really about the weather?
comprehension.a: It is a way of establishing that a conversation is possible — a safe opening nobody can be offended by and everybody can contribute to.
comprehension.why: Understanding the purpose changes what counts as a good reply. The subject is almost irrelevant; the exchange is the point.

comprehension.q: Somebody says cold today, isn't it. What is the expected reply?
comprehension.a: Agreement plus one small addition — yes, and it was so warm last week.
comprehension.why: The structure is fixed, which is what makes it rehearsable. Agreement alone is slightly flat; agreement plus an addition completes it.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say a full and accurate answer does not work?
comprehension.a: Because it treats an opening as a question, and the exchange stops.
comprehension.why: This is the inference that matters. Answering correctly can end a conversation, which is counter-intuitive for a learner trying to be accurate.

comprehension.q: What are the three language signals that tell a warning from a forecast?
comprehension.a: The modal verbs — will and may against do not and avoid; the hedging, which a forecast does constantly and a warning not at all; and the labelled heading with a level.
comprehension.why: Each signal is independently reliable, so a reader who catches any one of them knows which document they are holding.

comprehension.q: Why does a warning not hedge?
comprehension.a: Because the point of it is to be unambiguous — it is giving an instruction, not a probability.
comprehension.why: Hedging is appropriate to a prediction and inappropriate to an instruction. The absence of probably is itself information.

comprehension.q: The text says the last warning coming to nothing is not a reason to ignore the next one. Why?
comprehension.a: Because warnings are issued when the risk is high enough to act on even if the event does not happen — so a warning that comes to nothing has not failed.
comprehension.why: This is a point about how probability works rather than about weather, and the text names it as the most common mistake people make.

comprehension.q: You want to drive to the harbour at 21:00 on Thursday. What does the warning say, and what does the forecast add?
comprehension.a: The warning says do not travel on the coast road between Northfield and the harbour, and it is valid from 20:00. The forecast adds that the wind is strongest on the coast that evening, which is why.
comprehension.why: The warning gives the instruction and the forecast gives the reason. Reading only the warning tells you what; reading both tells you why, which helps you judge alternatives.

comprehension.q: What is the difference between AMBER and RED, and which one is this?
comprehension.a: AMBER means be prepared — a risk to travel and to property. RED means take action — a risk to life. This is AMBER.
comprehension.why: The levels are defined on the document itself, which is normal, and the difference is not a matter of degree — it is a different kind of risk.

comprehension.q: You planned to walk in the hills on Friday morning. Does anything in these two documents affect that?
comprehension.a: The warning ends at 06:00 Friday, so the wind is no longer covered. But the forecast says snow on the hills above 400 metres, which the warning never mentions.
comprehension.why: The document that seems more urgent does not cover this plan at all, and the one that seems merely informative does. Choosing the right document for the question is the skill being tested.

comprehension.q: The forecast says rain heavy in places. What does in places mean, and why does the warning contain no phrase like it?
comprehension.a: It means some areas will get heavy rain and others will not — it is hedging. The warning contains no hedging because it is giving an instruction rather than a prediction.
comprehension.why: The contrast between the two documents is visible in a single phrase, and it is exactly the signal Reading 2 describes.

grammar.title: Will: predicting, and deciding now
grammar.explanation: The easiest form in English to build, and it does two jobs. The second job is the one most courses leave out, and it is the one you will use in conversation.
grammar.rule:
FORM:  will + plain verb
  I will go.   She will go.   They will go.
  No -s, ever. Nothing changes.

CONTRACTIONS:
  I'll, she'll, we'll
  will not -> won't   (does not sound like will)

JOB 1 — PREDICTION
  It will rain tomorrow.
  The journey will take about two hours.

JOB 2 — DECIDING AS YOU SPEAK
  "The shop closes in ten minutes."
  "I'll go now."

AGAINST UNIT 10:
  arranged before   -> I'm leaving on Tuesday.
  decided this second -> I'll leave now.

HEDGING:
  It will probably rain.
  It definitely won't snow.
  probably goes AFTER will, BEFORE the verb.
grammar.workedExample:
Somebody tells you there are no more chairs in the room.
1. Did you plan anything before this moment? No. You are deciding right now.
2. Deciding as you speak takes will, not the present continuous.
3. Build it: will plus the plain verb. I will get some.
4. Contract it, because that is how it is actually said: I'll get some.
Now a prediction instead. You think it is going to rain tomorrow, but you are not certain.
1. This is a prediction, so will again.
2. Add hedging, because English rarely predicts flatly: probably.
3. Probably goes after will and before the verb: It will probably rain tomorrow.
The test that separates the two jobs: ask whether the decision existed before you opened your mouth. If it did, Unit 10's present continuous. If it did not, will.
grammar.mistake: Adding -s for he and she — she wills go, or she will goes. Nothing changes after will, ever. The other error is using will for something already arranged: I will leave on Tuesday, when you bought the ticket last week. That is an arrangement, and it takes the present continuous from Unit 10.
grammar.tip: Prediction, or decided this second. Nothing changes after will.
grammar.practice:
Write the sentence with will or won't.
1. A prediction: rain, tomorrow.
2. A prediction with probably: cold, at the weekend.
3. A negative prediction with definitely: snow, here.
4. Somebody says the shop closes soon. Decide to go now.
5. Somebody says we need more chairs. Offer to get them.
6. A prediction about a journey: about two hours.
grammar.answers:
1. It will rain tomorrow.
2. It will probably be cold at the weekend.
3. It definitely won't snow here.
4. I'll go now.
5. I'll get them.
6. The journey will take about two hours.
Numbers 4 and 5 are the second job — decisions made at the moment of speaking — and both are naturally contracted. If you wrote I will go now it is correct, but I'll go now is what you will actually hear and say.
In 2, probably sits after will and before be. In 3, definitely sits before won't, which is where it goes with a negative.

grammar.title: Describing a place
grammar.explanation: Three questions in a fixed order, and one structure that does most of the work. The structure is there is and there are, which you use for saying what exists somewhere.
grammar.rule:
THE ORDER:
  1  WHERE IT IS
       It's in the north of the country.
       It's on the coast.
       It's about fifty kilometres from the city.

  2  WHAT IS AROUND IT
       There are mountains behind it.
       There's a river through the middle.

  3  WHAT IT IS LIKE
       It's quite dry in summer.
       It's small and very quiet.

THERE IS / THERE ARE
  singular -> There is a river.
  plural   -> There are mountains.

PREPOSITIONS THAT GO WITH PLACES:
  IN the north OF the country
  TO the north OF the town
  ON the coast
  OFF the coast   (an island)
grammar.workedExample:
Describe a small town in a valley with hills around it, near the sea.
1. Where it is, first: It's in the south of the country, about ten kilometres from the sea.
2. What is around it, using there is and there are: It's in a valley, so there are hills on both sides, and there's a river through the middle.
3. What it is like, last: It's quite small — about four thousand people — and it's very quiet in winter.
Three sentences and a listener can picture it.
Notice the singular and plural: there are hills, because hills is plural, and there's a river, because river is singular. Getting that agreement right is the only grammatical decision in the whole pattern.
grammar.mistake: Using there is with a plural — there is mountains behind it. The verb agrees with what comes after it, not with there. The other common error is the prepositions: in the north of the country describes a region inside it, but to the north of the town means outside and beyond it. Those are different places and the two words are one letter apart in meaning.
grammar.tip: Where it is, what is around, what it is like. Singular is, plural are.
grammar.practice:
Write there is or there are, then describe the place in three sentences.
1. ____ a river through the middle.
2. ____ mountains behind the town.
3. ____ two lakes in the valley.
4. ____ a forest to the east.
5. ____ fields all around the village.
6. Describe a place you know, in three sentences, in the right order.
grammar.answers:
1. There is  2. There are  3. There are  4. There is  5. There are
6. Model: It's in the north of the country, about fifty kilometres from the coast. There are hills on three sides and there's a small river through the middle. It's quite dry in summer and very cold in winter.
In 1 to 5, look at the word straight after the gap: river and forest are singular, mountains, lakes and fields are plural. That word decides the verb every time.
Check your answer to 6 has all three parts, in order, and at least one there is or there are.

grammar.title: Because and so
grammar.explanation: Two words that join a reason to a result. They are opposite ways round, and that is the whole difficulty.
grammar.rule:
BECAUSE introduces the REASON (why)
  We stayed at home because it was raining.
                          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ reason

SO introduces the RESULT (what happened)
  It was raining, so we stayed at home.
                     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ result

Same two facts. Same meaning. Opposite order.

PUNCTUATION:
  so joining two sentences takes a comma before it
     It was raining, so we stayed at home.
  because in the middle takes no comma
     We stayed at home because it was raining.

NEVER BOTH IN ONE SENTENCE:
  Because it was raining, so we stayed at home.
  ^ wrong. Use one or the other.
grammar.workedExample:
You have two facts: the road was closed, and you were late.
1. Decide which is the reason and which is the result. The closed road is the reason; being late is what happened.
2. To put the reason second, use because: I was late because the road was closed.
3. To put the reason first, use so: The road was closed, so I was late.
Both are correct and they mean the same thing. Which you choose depends on what you want to say first.
The test that never fails: what comes after because answers why. What comes after so answers what happened. If you read your sentence and the thing after so is a reason, you have them the wrong way round.
grammar.mistake: Using both in one sentence — because it was raining, so we stayed at home. This is extremely common and it is wrong in English; one connector does the job and the second one has nothing left to join. The other error is swapping them, which reverses cause and effect: it was raining because we stayed at home says the staying caused the rain.
grammar.tip: After because comes why. After so comes what happened.
grammar.practice:
Join each pair twice — once with because and once with so.
1. It was raining. / We stayed at home.
2. The road was closed. / I was late.
3. There was fog. / The flight was cancelled.
4. It is very dry here. / Nothing grows.
grammar.answers:
1. We stayed at home because it was raining. / It was raining, so we stayed at home.
2. I was late because the road was closed. / The road was closed, so I was late.
3. The flight was cancelled because there was fog. / There was fog, so the flight was cancelled.
4. Nothing grows because it is very dry here. / It is very dry here, so nothing grows.
In every because version, the reason comes second. In every so version, the reason comes first. That is the only thing that changes.
Check your so sentences have a comma before so, and your because sentences do not have one.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — The weather exchange
speaking.instructions:
Say both sides of this exchange, then change the weather three times.
A: Cold today, isn't it.
B: Yes, and it was so warm last week.
A: I know. It'll probably rain later as well.
B: Probably.
That is a complete exchange. It is four lines and it is finished.
Record one full version. Then record a version where B gives the actual temperature instead, and listen to how the conversation stops.
speaking.tutor: Open a weather exchange with the tutor and try to keep it going for four turns without adding any real information.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Predicting
speaking.instructions:
Say eight predictions about the next week — the weather, your work, your journey, anything.
Four with will, two with will probably, two with definitely won't.
Record them. Play back and check nothing changed after will. If you hear she wills or she will goes, say those six sentences again.
speaking.tutor: Make eight predictions and ask the tutor which it thinks are most likely.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Deciding out loud
speaking.instructions:
Read each situation and respond out loud, immediately, with a decision using I'll.
The shop closes in ten minutes.
There are no more chairs.
Nobody has telephoned the supplier.
The last bus has gone.
It has started raining and the window is open.
There is nobody on the front desk.
Record all six.
The point of this drill is speed. If you had to think, do it again faster — these are decisions made at the moment of speaking, and hesitating changes what the form means.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to give you six situations and respond to each with an immediate I'll.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — A place you know
speaking.instructions:
Describe a place you know well — where you live now, where you grew up, or somewhere you have visited.
Three parts, in order: where it is, what is around it, what it is like.
Use there is and there are at least twice each.
Record it.
Then listen back and ask: could somebody find this place on a map from part one alone? If not, part one needs a distance or a direction from something bigger.
speaking.tutor: Describe a place to the tutor and ask it to say where it thinks the place is.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Because and so
speaking.instructions:
Take four pairs of facts from your own week — something that happened, and why.
Say each pair twice: once with because, once with so.
Record all eight sentences.
Play back and check that in every so sentence, the reason came first. If a reason ever followed so, you have the two words swapped.
speaking.tutor: Say four sentences with because and ask the tutor to turn each one round using so.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Read the forecast and the warning aloud
speaking.instructions:
Open Reading 3.
Read the whole forecast aloud, then the whole warning.
Listen to the difference in your own voice — the forecast hedges and the warning does not.
Then say aloud: whether you would drive to the harbour at nine on Thursday evening, and why.
Then say what the warning does not cover that the forecast does, for a walk in the hills on Friday morning.
Record the last two parts and keep them.
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor both documents and ask which one would change its plans.

writing.title: Writing 1 — A place described in three parts
writing.prompt:
Describe a place you know well.
Three paragraphs, one for each part: where it is, what is around it, what it is like.
Use there is and there are at least twice each.
Use at least four words from the land and water groups.
Then underline every there is and there are and check the singular and plural agree.
writing.model:
It's in the north of the country, in a valley about fifty kilometres from the coast. The nearest big town is an hour away by bus, and the road follows the river most of the way.
There are hills on both sides, quite steep ones, and there's a river through the middle of the town. There are fields all along the valley floor, and above them there's forest on the north side where it is too steep to farm. There is a lake about three kilometres to the east.
It's quite dry in summer and very cold in winter, because of the hills. It's a small place — about four thousand people — and it's very quiet after about eight in the evening. In winter there's often fog in the valley in the morning, so the sun does not reach the town until nearly ten.
writing.criteria: Three paragraphs matching the three parts in order; at least two there is and two there are, each agreeing correctly; at least four land or water words; part one gives a direction or a distance from something bigger
writing.support: Draw the place before you write it — a rough map with the town in the middle and whatever is around it marked. Paragraph 2 then writes itself, and the agreement errors become visible because you can see what is singular and what is plural.
writing.extension: Rewrite paragraph 3 for somebody deciding whether to move there. What did you add, and what did you leave out?

writing.title: Writing 2 — A forecast and a warning for the same day
writing.prompt:
Invent one day of bad weather.
Write two documents about it.
First a forecast: morning, afternoon and evening, using will, and hedging at least three times with probably, mainly, in places or at times.
Then a warning for the same day: a level, a period of validity, and at least three instructions.
The warning must contain no hedging at all.
writing.model:
FORECAST — Saturday
MORNING  Fog in the valley, clearing by about ten. Cold, 3 degrees.
AFTERNOON  Cloud increasing from the west. Rain arriving after two, heavy in places. 8 degrees.
EVENING  Rain continuing and probably turning to snow above 300 metres. Wind strengthening, strongest in the north. 4 degrees.

** WEATHER WARNING — AMBER **
Issued 17:00 Saturday. Valid 19:00 Saturday to 08:00 Sunday.
SNOW AND STRONG WIND
Do not travel on the mountain road.
Avoid parking under trees.
Some power cuts are likely.
Bus services north of the river are cancelled until further notice.
writing.criteria: Forecast has three parts of the day, uses will, and hedges at least three times; warning has a level, a validity period and at least three instructions; warning contains no hedging words at all; the two documents describe the same weather
writing.support: Write the forecast first and then go through the warning deleting every hedge you accidentally wrote. That deletion is the exercise — the difference between the two documents is almost entirely which words you are allowed to use.
writing.extension: Write a third version: a message to one friend telling them what to do. Which of the two documents does it sound more like, and why?

writing.title: Writing 3 — Read the forecast and the warning
writing.prompt:
Use the forecast and warning in Reading 3. Write full-sentence answers.
1. You want to drive to the harbour at 21:00 on Thursday. What does the warning say, and what does the forecast add?
2. What is the difference between AMBER and RED?
3. You planned to walk in the hills on Friday morning. Does anything affect that, and which document says so?
4. The forecast says heavy in places. What does that mean, and why is there nothing like it in the warning?
5. Somebody says the last warning came to nothing, so this one can be ignored. Answer them.
writing.model:
1. The warning says do not travel on the coast road between Northfield and the harbour, and it is valid from 20:00, so it covers 21:00. The forecast adds the reason: the wind is strengthening from the west and is strongest on the coast that evening.
2. AMBER means be prepared — there is a risk to travel and to property. RED means take action — there is a risk to life. They are different kinds of risk, not different amounts.
3. Yes. The warning ends at 06:00 Friday so it does not cover the walk, but the forecast says snow on the hills above 400 metres, which the warning never mentions.
4. It means some areas will get heavy rain and others will not — it is hedging. The warning has nothing like it because it is giving instructions, and an instruction that hedges is not usable.
5. A warning is issued when the risk is high enough to act on even if the event does not happen, so a warning that came to nothing has not failed. Judging the next one by the last one is exactly the mistake Reading 2 describes.
writing.criteria: Five answers, each a full sentence; answer 1 uses both documents; answer 3 identifies that the more urgent document does not cover the plan; answer 5 explains the probability point rather than restating the warning
writing.support: Before answering, write down the validity period of the warning and the four parts of the forecast. Three of the five questions turn on whether a time falls inside the warning or outside it.
writing.extension: Write a sixth question that neither document answers, and say where you would look.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the eight mistakes
writing.prompt:
Every sentence has exactly one mistake from this unit.
Write each out correctly and say which pattern it came from.
1. She will goes tomorrow.
2. It will rain probably tomorrow.
3. Because it was raining, so we stayed at home.
4. It was raining because we stayed at home.
5. There is mountains behind the town.
6. It is a small town in the coast.
7. I will leave on Tuesday. (you bought the ticket last week)
8. It is quite dry in summer. There is fields all around.
writing.model:
1. She will go tomorrow. (Pattern 1 — nothing changes after will)
2. It will probably rain tomorrow. (Pattern 1 — probably goes after will and before the verb)
3. It was raining, so we stayed at home. (Pattern 3 — never both connectors in one sentence)
4. We stayed at home because it was raining. (Pattern 3 — the two were swapped, which reversed cause and effect)
5. There are mountains behind the town. (Pattern 2 — plural takes there are)
6. It is a small town on the coast. (Pattern 2 — places on the coast take on)
7. I am leaving on Tuesday. (Pattern 1 — already arranged, so the present continuous from Unit 10)
8. It is quite dry in summer. There are fields all around. (Pattern 2 — fields is plural)
writing.criteria: All eight corrected; each labelled with the right pattern; number 4 corrects the meaning rather than the grammar; number 7 changes tense rather than fixing will
writing.support: Numbers 3 and 4 are the same two facts going wrong in two different ways — one uses both connectors, the other uses one connector backwards. Fix them together and the rule becomes clear.
writing.extension: Number 4 was grammatically perfect and said something absurd. Write two more like it, where swapping because and so reverses cause and effect.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Will, won't, probably
activities.instructions:
Complete each sentence with will, won't, will probably or definitely won't.
1. It ____ rain tomorrow. (a plain prediction)
2. It ____ be cold at the weekend. (you think so, not certain)
3. It ____ snow here. (you are certain it will not)
4. The journey ____ take about two hours.
5. "The shop closes in ten minutes." "I ____ go now."
6. "We need more chairs." "I ____ get them."
7. She ____ be here before six. (she is never early)
8. The fog ____ clear by ten. (you think so)
9. It ____ be hot at midday.
10. "Nobody has telephoned the supplier." "I ____ do it."
11. The storm ____ pass by morning. (you think so)
12. There ____ be any snow this year. (you are certain)
activities.answers:
1. will  2. will probably  3. definitely won't  4. will  5. will  6. will  7. definitely won't  8. will probably  9. will  10. will  11. will probably  12. definitely won't
Numbers 5, 6 and 10 are the second job — decisions made as you speak. All three would normally be contracted to I'll in real speech.
Check the position of probably in 2, 8 and 11: it comes after will and before the verb. And definitely comes before won't in 3, 7 and 12.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Because or so?
activities.instructions:
Choose because or so.
1. We stayed at home ____ it was raining.
2. It was raining, ____ we stayed at home.
3. The road was closed, ____ I was late.
4. I was late ____ the road was closed.
5. Nothing grows here ____ it is very dry.
6. It is very dry here, ____ nothing grows.
7. The flight was cancelled ____ there was fog.
8. There was fog, ____ the flight was cancelled.
9. It is colder in the valley ____ the sun does not reach it until ten.
10. The ferry was cancelled, ____ we drove instead.
11. We drove instead ____ the ferry was cancelled.
12. There is a warning, ____ do not use the coast road.
activities.answers:
1. because  2. so  3. so  4. because  5. because  6. so  7. because  8. so  9. because  10. so  11. because  12. so
The pairs 1-2, 3-4, 5-6, 7-8 and 10-11 are the same facts each way round. In every because sentence the reason comes second; in every so sentence the reason comes first.
The test: read the words after the connector. If they answer why, it is because. If they answer what happened, it is so.
Number 9 is worth a second look — the sun not reaching the valley is the reason it is colder, not the result.

activities.title: Practice 3 — There is or there are?
activities.instructions:
Write there is or there are.
1. ____ a river through the middle.
2. ____ mountains behind the town.
3. ____ two lakes in the valley.
4. ____ a forest to the east.
5. ____ fields all around the village.
6. ____ fog in the valley most mornings.
7. ____ three bridges over the river.
8. ____ a beach south of the town.
9. ____ hills on both sides.
10. ____ a lot of cloud this morning.
11. ____ no shops in the village.
12. ____ snow on the mountains all year.
activities.answers:
1. There is  2. There are  3. There are  4. There is  5. There are  6. There is  7. There are  8. There is  9. There are  10. There is  11. There are  12. There is
Look at the word straight after the gap. That word, not there, decides the verb.
Numbers 6, 10 and 12 are the ones people get wrong: fog, cloud and snow are uncountable, so they take is even though they feel like a lot of something.
Number 11 takes are because shops is plural, even though the sentence is negative.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Describe four places
activities.instructions:
Describe each place in three sentences — where it is, what is around it, what it is like.
Use there is or there are at least once in each.
1. A town in a valley with hills around it.
2. A village on the coast.
3. A place in a very dry area.
4. An island.
5. Where you live now.
6. Where you grew up.
activities.answers:
Model answers for 1 to 4 — yours will differ, and should.
1. It's in the north, about fifty kilometres from the city. There are hills on both sides and there's a river through the middle. It's quite cold in winter and there is often fog in the morning.
2. It's a small village on the east coast, about an hour from the nearest town. There's a beach to the south and there are fields behind it. It's very windy, and it's almost empty in winter.
3. It's in the south of the country, on the edge of the desert. There are no rivers near it and there is very little rain. It's extremely hot in the day and quite cold at night.
4. It's a small island off the west coast. There are about two hundred people on it and there's one road. You can only get there by boat, so it's very quiet.
Check each of yours: part one gives a direction or a distance, part two uses there is or there are with correct agreement, part three says what it is like rather than what is in it.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Read a real forecast
activities.instructions:
Find a real weather forecast for where you are — on a screen, in a newspaper, or spoken.
Write down: every use of will, every hedging word, and the temperature for each part of the day.
Then write your own one-sentence prediction for tomorrow, using will probably.
The next day, check whether you were right.
activities.answers:
No key — it is your forecast.
What most people find: forecasts hedge far more than they expect. In a short forecast there are usually four or five hedging words — probably, mainly, in places, at times, becoming — and almost nothing is stated flatly.
The second finding is that will appears less often than you would think, because forecasts also use becoming, turning and a lot of noun phrases with no verb at all: rain in the north, fog clearing. Those are worth noticing, because they are the most compressed English you will read anywhere.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Open a weather exchange
activities.instructions:
This week, open one conversation with a stranger about the weather.
A queue, a bus stop, a waiting room — anywhere people are already standing together.
Use the shape from Speaking 1: a short comment, then agreement plus one addition.
Write three lines: what you said, what they said, and how long the exchange lasted.
activities.answers:
No key.
What most people find: the exchange is shorter than expected and that is correct. Four lines is a complete weather conversation and stopping there is not a failure.
The second finding is that agreement is almost always returned. This is the most predictable exchange in English, which is exactly why it is worth using as your first conversation with a stranger — the risk of it going wrong is close to zero, and the practice is real.

options: She will goes tomorrow.
She wills go tomorrow.
She will go tomorrow.
She will to go tomorrow.
quizzes.why: Nothing changes after will — no -s, no to, and no change to the verb. It is the simplest form in English to build.

quizzes.q: Somebody says the shop closes in ten minutes and you decide at that moment to go. What do you say?
options: I'll go now.
I am going now.
I go now.
I will going now.
quizzes.why: A decision made at the moment of speaking takes will. If you had arranged it earlier it would be the present continuous from Unit 10.

options: It probably will rain — always.
It will rain probably.
Probably it will rain — the only correct place.
It will probably rain.
quizzes.why: Probably sits after will and before the verb. You will also hear it probably will rain, and neither causes a problem, but this is the standard position.

options: There is mountains behind the town.
There have mountains behind the town.
There are mountains behind the town.
It has mountains behind the town.
quizzes.a: There are mountains behind the town.
quizzes.why: The verb agrees with the word after it, not with there. Mountains is plural, so it takes are.

options: It is a small town on the coast.
It is a small town in the coast.
It is a small town at the coast.
It is a small town to the coast.
quizzes.a: It is a small town on the coast.
quizzes.why: Places beside the sea take on the coast. An island takes off the coast, which means separated from it by water.

options: Because it was raining, so we stayed at home.
It was raining, so we stayed at home.
So it was raining, because we stayed at home.
It was raining because we stayed at home.
quizzes.a: It was raining, so we stayed at home.
quizzes.why: One connector does the job. Using both is a very common error, and swapping them reverses cause and effect.

options: The reason
The result
Either one
The time
quizzes.why: After because comes why. After so comes what happened. That is the whole rule and it decides every case.

quizzes.q: Which sentence uses there is correctly?
options: There is three bridges over the river.
There is hills on both sides.
There is fields all around.
There is fog in the valley most mornings.
quizzes.a: There is fog in the valley most mornings.
quizzes.why: Fog is uncountable, so it takes is. The other three all have plural nouns after the gap and need there are.

quizzes.q: What is the difference between a forecast and a warning?
options: A forecast is longer than a warning
A forecast is spoken; a warning is written
A forecast predicts; a warning instructs
A forecast is official; a warning is not
quizzes.a: A forecast predicts; a warning instructs
quizzes.why: A forecast uses will and hedges constantly. A warning uses do not and avoid, and does not hedge at all, because an instruction that hedges is not usable.

quizzes.q: The forecast says rain heavy in places. What does in places mean?
options: Everywhere in the region
Some areas will get it and others will not
Only in towns
For a short time only
quizzes.a: Some areas will get it and others will not
quizzes.why: It is hedging — the forecast is stating a probability rather than a certainty. This is exactly the kind of phrase a warning never contains.

quizzes.q: AMBER means be prepared and RED means take action. What is the difference?
options: Red lasts longer
Amber is for wind and red is for snow
Red covers a bigger area
Amber is a risk to travel and property; red is a risk to life
quizzes.a: Amber is a risk to travel and property; red is a risk to life
quizzes.why: They are different kinds of risk, not different amounts of the same risk. The document defines both levels on itself, which is normal.

quizzes.q: Somebody says the last warning came to nothing, so this one can be ignored. What is wrong with that?
options: The last warning was a different colour
Warnings are issued when the risk is high enough to act on even if nothing happens
Warnings are always correct
The last warning was not official
quizzes.a: Warnings are issued when the risk is high enough to act on even if nothing happens
quizzes.why: A warning that came to nothing has not failed — it stated a risk, not a certainty. Reading 2 names this as the most common mistake people make with warnings.

teacherNotes.note: Three pattern cards, each with a worked example, and every exercise has an answer key. Practice 2 is the diagnostic and it is built as five reversible pairs so the learner can see the rule from their own answers. Practices 5 and 6 are field tasks with no key, and both carry a what-most-people-find note so a solo learner still gets feedback.

teacherNotes.type: Will does two jobs and both are taught here
teacherNotes.note: Prediction is the use every course teaches; the decision-at-the-moment-of-speaking use is the one learners actually need in conversation and rarely meet. Speaking 3 drills it under time pressure on purpose, because hesitating before I'll changes what the form communicates. Unit 15 contrasts will with going to and the present continuous and does not re-teach any of them.

teacherNotes.type: Weather talk is a social skill, not a topic
teacherNotes.note: Reading 1 exists to explain why an accurate answer can end a conversation. Learners often avoid these exchanges as content-free small talk, when they are in fact the most rehearsable conversations in English — fixed subject, fixed structure, agreement almost always correct. Practice 6 asks for one real attempt, and four lines is a complete success.

teacherNotes.type: Because and so are swapped more often than they are missed
teacherNotes.note: The error that matters is not omission but reversal, which produces grammatical sentences that say something absurd — it was raining because we stayed at home. Writing 4 number 4 is that error deliberately, and its extension asks the learner to write two more, because producing the absurd version is what makes the direction memorable. The both-connectors error in number 3 is separately very common and worth naming as its own mistake.

teacherNotes.type: Why a forecast and a warning together
teacherNotes.note: The two documents are the clearest available example of register doing real work: the same weather described twice, once hedged and once not. Four of the ten comprehension questions turn on which document covers a given time, and one turns on the more urgent-looking document not covering the plan at all. Writing 2 asks learners to produce both, and the deletion of accidental hedges from the warning is where the learning happens.

The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner and no task here is scored by it alone. Writing 1 and Speaking 4 ask learners to describe where they live or grew up: their actual address, and any detail specific enough to locate their home, must never be collected, shared or entered into the app. The tasks ask for a place at town or village scale, and that framing should stay. Practice 6 involves approaching a stranger, and learners should be reminded to choose a public setting where people are already waiting together.

selfAssessment.statement: I can say what I think will happen, and decide something out loud as I speak.
I can describe a place — where it is, what is around it, and what it is like.
I can say we stayed at home because it was raining, and turn it round with so.
I can read a weather forecast and a warning and know which one tells me to change my plans.

assignment.title: A place described, and two documents read
assignment.instructions: Two parts. First, record a three-part description of a place you know — where it is, what is around it, what it is like — using there is and there are at least twice each, then record eight predictions about the coming week using will, will probably and definitely won't. Second, write full-sentence answers to the five questions in Writing 3 about the forecast and warning in Reading 3, and add your own forecast and warning for one invented day of bad weather, with the warning containing no hedging at all. Keep both together.
assignment.submissionType: An audio recording and written answers
